facts.statement: The study was a randomized, double-blind trial in which 52 people with Parkinson's disease and freezing of gait were assigned to either real or fake brain stimulation.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Data from 50 participants, 26 who got real stimulation and 24 who got fake stimulation, were analyzed.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The main measure was how much a questionnaire score about freezing of gait changed after the treatment.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Researchers also tracked movement scores, walking measurements, and brain activity using functional MRI.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: People who received real stimulation had a larger drop in their freezing of gait score than those who received fake stimulation, and this difference was still present four weeks later.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Real stimulation led to early improvements in movement, balance, and walking speed and step length, which were still seen at the four-week follow-up.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Brain scans showed stronger connections between two brain regions during a mental walking task, and this was linked to better clinical and walking results.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Symptoms other than movement, such as mood or thinking, also improved and stayed better at the four-week check.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The authors suggest this treatment has short-term potential for freezing of gait and related mental symptoms when patients are off their medication.
facts.subject: humans
